This cell is a CONSERVATIVE placement built from Cosmos's thermal class (a warm-season, heat-tolerant annual) plus the general TAMU AgriLife frost-free Valley season model, not a stated Cosmos RGV planting date.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring set-out is placed in early March, shortly after the Valley's rare-frost date (~late February); a second, fall set-out is placed in early October. harvest_end.label: primary

basil.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow basil in two arms: spring (set out in early March, shortly after the Valley's rare late-February frost date) and fall (set out mid-September into mid-October). Skip planting new basil in the peak of summer: the Valley's heat and humidity bring on a leaf disease called downy mildew, so older plants decline in July and August even though it never frosts here. Basil does not have its own Rio Grande Valley planting chart from Texas A&M AgriLife, so this window is a conservative placement built from its thermal class and general frost-free Valley timing, not a source-stated RGV date. Water at the base of the plant, never overhead, and look for mildew-resistant varieties.
basil.region_notes_seasoned: Basil is not covered in either TAMU AgriLife RGV vegetable planting table, so this cell is CONSERVATIVE: authored from basil's thermal class (a warm-season, frost-tender herb prone to downy mildew in humid heat) plus the general TAMU AgriLife frost-free Valley season model, mirroring the season_over (not heat_pause) summer gap already authored on basil's own fl_peninsula cell for the same disease-driven reason. Spring set-out is placed in early March, just after the Valley's rare late-February frost date, with harvest running into June; a fall set-out follows mid-September into mid-October as peak-summer humidity eases, with harvest continuing through the mild Valley winter. July and August are a genuine planting and quality gap here, not a frost gap: the Valley's heat and humidity strongly favor basil downy mildew. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10.

Skip planting Borage from spring through summer: Valley heat keeps it from growing and blooming well.
borage.region_notes_seasoned: Borage in the RGV runs on the winter-garden calendar: set out Oct 1 through Nov 15, with bloom running through the mild Valley winter. heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Chives are a cool-preferring perennial that grows best in mild weather. The Rio Grande Valley's summer runs hotter and drier than the Florida peninsula's, so this cell adopts chives's own fl_peninsula heat_pause precedent (rather than mirroring the no-pause hawaii_tropical shape used elsewhere in this cell) as the more climate-analogous, more conservative choice for a hot-summer subtropical climate. In the Valley's extreme summer heat the plants slow, the foliage scorches, and many clumps go semi-dormant, so the cutting calendar pauses through the hottest months and picks back up as the weather cools. Clumps already in the ground are best carried with afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water. The exact pause months are modeled from chives's own fl_peninsula evidence and the Valley's summer heat pattern, not a chives-specific Valley chart.
